line.bridge: Vary the line. Vary the sentence. A change in length can change the rhythm.
before: The rain fell. The path darkened. We walked on. The wind rose.
after: Rain darkened the path as we walked toward the river.
Then the wind rose.

game.prompt: Build the longer sentence beginning with As, then give the short ending its own line.
game.reason: The As clause establishes the background. The short final sentence changes the pace.

vocab.meaning: Thick and thin lines vary visual emphasis; different sentence lengths vary prose rhythm.
A conjunction can connect clauses into a continuous thought.
A line can divide areas; a full stop separates complete sentences.

notes: Sentence length is an analogy for line variation, not a rule that longer sentences are better.
In a complex sentence, a dependent clause needs a main clause.

levels.A2: One long sentence. One short sentence. Listen to the rhythm.
levels.B1: As connects the background action to the rain-darkened path. The short ending changes the pace.
levels.B2: Sentence variety shapes narrative rhythm; a short sentence can gain emphasis after a longer one.

color.bridge: A palette colors what we see. Diction colors how a narrator presents a scene.
before: The room was empty and quiet.
after: The room was deserted and silent.

game.prompt: The narrator wants the empty room to feel unsettling. Which word pair best supports that intention?
game.reason: Deserted and silent can suggest unease in this context. Peaceful and still suggest calm; busy and crowded change the basic scene.
variants: The empty room felt peaceful and still.
The room was deserted and silent.
The room was busy and crowded.

vocab.meaning: Both can suggest an inviting mood in this context.
Both can reduce intensity; audience and setting matter.
Related hues create a palette; word associations help create a verbal tone.

notes: A word’s connotation is an association beyond its basic meaning. The effect depends on audience and context.
Deserted does not always imply fear, and silent does not always imply danger. Here, the narrator’s intended mood supplies the context.

levels.A2: Empty and deserted both suggest no people here. Peaceful suggests calm.
levels.B1: The basic scene stays similar, but the connotations change its mood.
levels.B2: Diction colors the narrator’s presentation of the scene. Reader response still depends on the surrounding prose.

shape.bridge: Read this as a story first. Then reveal the thematic echoes around the moment that changes Leena’s response.
before: Leena was certain she could repair the radio alone. When her brother offered a suggestion, she spoke over him. She tightened her grip on the screwdriver and tried the same screw once more. “I only want to hear Mum’s song again,” he said. She loosened her grip and set the screwdriver down. This time, she listened as he pointed to a loose wire. Together, they brought the music back.
after: Leena was certain she could repair the radio alone.
When her brother offered a suggestion, she spoke over him.
She tightened her grip on the screwdriver and tried the same screw once more.
“I only want to hear Mum’s song again,” he said.
She loosened her grip and set the screwdriver down.
This time, she listened as he pointed to a loose wire.
Together, they brought the music back.

game.prompt: Rebuild the story in logical order: she tries alone, resists help, hears why the music matters, and learns to work with her brother.
tiles: Leena was certain she could repair the radio alone.
When her brother offered a suggestion, she spoke over him.
She tightened her grip on the screwdriver and tried the same screw once more.
“I only want to hear Mum’s song again,” he said.
She loosened her grip and set the screwdriver down.
This time, she listened as he pointed to a loose wire.
Together, they brought the music back.
game.reason: The story moves naturally from a failed solo attempt to cooperation. Alone and together frame it; speaking over and listening form another pair; gripping and releasing the tool frame the brother’s reminder of their shared purpose.

vocab.meaning: Thematic counterparts return in reverse order around a central turn.
The brother’s wish to hear Mum’s song shifts the scene from a contest toward a shared purpose.
Alone / together, speaking / listening, and holding on / letting go correspond through meaning, rather than through repeated locations.

notes: The seven sentences form one naturally ordered prose paragraph. Indentation is an analytical display; the words and chronology stay the same.
Thematic correspondence can use development or contrast, rather than identical wording. Here, self-reliance changes into cooperation and control makes room for openness.
This is an authored chiastic or concentric narrative example, not a rule that every narrative must follow. Terms for larger mirrored structures vary.

levels.A2: First she tries alone. Then she listens. In the end, they work together.
levels.B1: Alone matches together; speaking over him matches listening; a tight grip matches letting go. The song reminds them of a shared purpose.
levels.B2: The narrative’s thematic correspondences are A: self-reliance, B: speaking, C: control, X: shared purpose, C′: openness, B′: listening, A′: cooperation. Indentation reveals this analysis without changing the prose or event order.

texture.bridge: Look at a surface. Listen to a sentence. Both can have a noticeable texture.
before: The stream moved over stones and made a quiet sound.
after: The stream slipped softly over smooth stones.

game.prompt: Build the flowing description. Follow the stream’s movement over the stones.
game.reason: Stream, slipped, softly, smooth, and stones repeat an initial s sound. The sound pattern gives the description a noticeable texture.

vocab.meaning: These describe an impression, not a universally fixed effect.
Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds in nearby words.
Cadence is the rise, fall, and rhythm of speech.

notes: Alliteration repeats sounds, not simply letters. Assonance repeats vowel sounds.
Read both versions aloud. A sound pattern can be memorable without always being suitable.

levels.A2: Hear the s sounds. Slipped softly suggests gentle movement.
levels.B1: Repeated initial consonant sounds create alliteration in this description.
levels.B2: Alliteration, stress, and phrasing contribute to the sentence’s cadence. Sound supports the scene rather than merely decorating it.

form.bridge: Shading suggests visual depth. Context can suggest meaning beneath the spoken words.
before: Mina glanced at her guest’s coat.
“You’re leaving already?” she asked.
after: Mina glanced at her guest’s coat.
“You’re leaving already?” she asked.
Possible subtext: she wants the guest to stay longer.

game.prompt: The guest has picked up a coat. Mina says, “You’re leaving already?” What might she be implying?
tiles: She may want the guest to stay longer.
She is confirming a printed departure timetable.
She is giving directions to a bus stop.
game.reason: Already and the glance at the coat support a possible wish for the guest to stay. The line does not prove that intention.

vocab.meaning: A flat picture can suggest depth; a sentence in context can suggest more than it states.
This is what you can directly see or what the sentence explicitly says.
Subtext is an implied meaning supported by context.

notes: An implication is an interpretation, not a guaranteed hidden message. Ask or check when the stakes matter.
People in every culture can use indirect language; avoid assuming everyone in a country communicates in the same way.

levels.A2: She asks about leaving. She may want the guest to stay.
levels.B1: Already and the surrounding action help us infer a possible unstated feeling.
levels.B2: Subtext emerges from dialogue in context. It remains an interpretation; another tone of voice could support a different reading.

space.bridge: Empty areas make room around visual elements. Breaks and omission create pauses within prose.
before: He raised his hand to knock. He heard a voice inside. His hand fell. He waited.
after: He raised his hand to knock. He heard a voice inside. His hand fell.
He waited.

game.prompt: Give “He waited.” its own paragraph so that the final pause stands out.
tiles: He raised his hand to knock.
game.reason: The break separates the final wait from the preceding action. It can make the pause more noticeable without adding an explanation.

vocab.meaning: Both can separate groups and make relationships easier to see.
A break gives the reader a visible pause before a new group.
Leaving something out can carry meaning, but essential details must stay.

notes: This task asks for a particular pacing choice; several other paragraph arrangements are possible.
A pause can suggest tension without proving the character’s reason. Omission should leave enough context for the intended reading.

levels.A2: The final sentence stands alone. Pause before you read it.
levels.B1: A paragraph break changes the pacing without changing the words.
levels.B2: The unstated reason for his hesitation leaves room for inference. White space and omission contribute differently to that effect.

typography.bridge: Type directs the eye. Stress, emphasis, and register shape the voice of prose.
before: She said she had seen him leave.
after: She said she had seen HIM leave.

game.prompt: The narrator is correcting who she saw: that man, rather than someone else. Which word should receive stress?
game.reason: Stress him to contrast that person with someone else. Stress on she or leave would shift the point of contrast.
variants: SHE said she had seen him leave.
She said she had seen HIM leave.
She said she had seen him LEAVE.

vocab.meaning: Both can direct attention to a particular part.
Register is language suited to an audience and situation.
Formatting can mark emphasis, but too much emphasis makes everything compete.

notes: Serif and sans serif do not map rigidly onto formal and casual writing. Context and the particular typeface matter.
Use formatting to support meaning; do not rely on color or styling alone to communicate essential information.

levels.A2: Stress him. The important difference is the person.
levels.B1: The same words can emphasize who spoke, who was seen, or what happened.
levels.B2: Spoken stress and written emphasis can focus a contrast. Register also shapes a narrative voice through vocabulary and phrasing.

contrast.bridge: Visible differences attract attention. Opposed ideas can make a sentence memorable.
before: Outside, the street was crowded. Inside, the house was quiet.
after: Outside, the street roared.
Inside, the house whispered.

game.prompt: Rebuild the opposed descriptions: Outside first, then Inside.
game.reason: Outside and inside frame opposing sound impressions. Roared and whispered personify the places; they suggest loudness and quietness.

vocab.meaning: Both create a relationship through difference.
Antithesis places contrasting ideas in a parallel structure.
Juxtaposition places things beside each other so the reader can compare them.

notes: The street and house do not literally speak. Roared and whispered are figurative descriptions.
Antithesis places opposed ideas in a parallel structure. Juxtaposition is a broader technique of placing things together for comparison.

levels.A2: Roared suggests a loud sound. Whispered suggests a quiet sound.
levels.B1: The matching clause pattern makes the outside / inside contrast clear.
levels.B2: Antithesis and parallel structure sharpen the comparison; personification gives each setting a voice.

authentic.quote: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times,
authentic.author: Charles Dickens
authentic.work: A Tale of Two Cities, opening sentence (1859)
authentic.notice: Excerpt: best / worst are opposed within a repeated sentence pattern.

hierarchy.bridge: A visual layout has levels of importance. A prose paragraph connects its main point, explanation, and support.
before: A quiet desk can make it easier to focus.
A student might read a chapter away from street noise.
A library can be a useful place to study.
after: A library can be a useful place to study.
A quiet desk can make it easier to focus.
For example, a student might read a chapter away from street noise.

game.prompt: Build an explanatory paragraph: main point → explanation → example.
tiles: A library can be a useful place to study.
A quiet desk can make it easier to focus.
For example, a student might read a chapter away from street noise.
game.reason: The first sentence states the main point. The second explains it; For example introduces a supporting illustration.

vocab.meaning: Both tell the reader what matters first.
Supporting information develops the main point.
A quick notice often benefits from giving the key answer early.

notes: This is one common explanatory structure, not a compulsory order for every paragraph.
A narrative may delay its main point; an argument may need evidence beyond an illustrative example.

levels.A2: First the main idea. Then a reason. Then an example.
levels.B1: The topic sentence organizes the explanation and supporting example.
levels.B2: The paragraph’s hierarchy connects its main claim to explanation and illustration. Longer essays can repeat this relationship across sections.

alignment.bridge: Shared edges organize visual blocks. Shared grammatical forms organize verbal blocks.
before: She wanted to read the story,
understanding the ending,
and an explanation of the characters.
after: She wanted to read the story,
understand the ending,
and explain the characters.

game.prompt: Align the three actions after “She wanted to”: read → understand → explain.
tiles: She wanted to read the story,
game.reason: Read, understand, and explain share the same grammatical form after wanted to. Each names an action in the list.

vocab.meaning: Both establish a consistent organizing pattern.
Match verbs with verbs or noun phrases with noun phrases.
Both help organize relationships between parts.

notes: Parallel grammar does not require phrases of equal length.
Consistency in tense and terminology can help, while purposeful variation is still possible.

levels.A2: Read, understand, explain: three matching verbs.
levels.B1: The shared wanted to applies to all three parallel verbs.
levels.B2: Parallelism aligns grammatical units; the phrases need not have equal length or identical content.

authentic.quote: of the people, by the people, for the people
authentic.author: Abraham Lincoln
authentic.notice: Excerpt: each phrase uses preposition + the people. The phrase lengths match here, but parallelism does not require equal length.

balance.bridge: Visual weight can be distributed across a layout. Punctuation can connect or interrupt the weight of ideas.
before: The journey was long. The conversation was short.
after: The journey was long; the conversation was short.

game.prompt: Connect these related independent clauses with a semicolon.
game.reason: Each clause can stand as a sentence. The semicolon holds the related statements together; the long / short contrast creates a balanced rhetorical impression.

vocab.meaning: Paired clauses can create a balanced rhetorical impression.
An em dash can introduce an interruption or an added thought.
A periodic sentence delays its main clause; a loose sentence gives it early.

notes: The semicolon comparison is a teaching analogy. Independent clauses need not have equal length or importance.
An em dash has several uses and is not inherently asymmetrical.

levels.A2: Each side is a complete sentence. Read a small pause at the semicolon.
levels.B1: The semicolon links related independent clauses without a conjunction.
levels.B2: Compare the balanced clauses with a delayed main clause: Although the journey was long, the conversation was short.

proximity.bridge: Nearby items look related. Related ideas belong together; language makes their connection explicit.
before: At dawn, Lina reached the river.
The boat’s blue paint was peeling.
Mist covered the water.
Inside the boat, a rope lay beside the oar.
after: At dawn, Lina reached the river. Mist covered the water.
The boat’s blue paint was peeling. Inside the boat, a rope lay beside the oar.

game.prompt: Group the scene into two paragraphs: the riverside setting, then the details of the boat.
tiles: At dawn, Lina reached the river.
The boat’s blue paint was peeling.
Inside the boat, a rope lay beside the oar.
game.reason: Dawn, the river, and mist establish the setting. Paint, rope, and oar develop the boat. Grouping gives the reader a clear focus for each paragraph.

vocab.meaning: A paragraph holds related ideas together.
A break can mark a change in topic.
Words such as however, also, and this can show relationships when their references are clear.

notes: A cohesive word cannot repair unrelated ideas by itself.
This needs a clear referent. Name the noun when several things could be meant.

levels.A2: Put the setting together. Put the boat details together.
levels.B1: Related sentences share a paragraph. The break signals a shift in descriptive focus.
levels.B2: Paragraphing helps coherence; repeated references to river, water, and boat help create cohesion within the scene.

repetition.bridge: Repeating a visual feature creates a pattern. Repeating selected words can create a verbal pattern.
before: She remembered the narrow path, the empty bench, and the quiet house.
after: She remembered the narrow path.
She remembered the empty bench.
She remembered the quiet house.

game.prompt: Rebuild the memory sequence: path → bench → house. Keep the repeated opening.
game.reason: She remembered repeats at the start of successive sentences. This anaphora frames three memories in the requested sequence.

vocab.meaning: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive units.
A refrain returns at intervals.
The same phrase or idea frames the opening and ending.

notes: Purposeful repetition can create emphasis; accidental repetition can make prose cumbersome.
Bookending example: The river kept its secrets. … The river kept its secrets. The intervening passage develops what that returning line means.

levels.A2: Hear She remembered at the start of each sentence.
levels.B1: The repeated opening unifies separate memories and gives them a rhythm.
levels.B2: Anaphora repeats openings; a refrain returns at intervals; inclusio frames a passage with a returning phrase or idea.

simplicity.bridge: Remove extra decoration. Remove extra wording. Keep the information the audience needs.
before: He took a deep breath in order to calm himself.
after: He took a deep breath to calm himself.

game.prompt: Keep the action and its purpose. Remove the two-word phrase that adds no meaning here.
game.reason: Removing in order preserves what he did and why: He took a deep breath to calm himself.

vocab.meaning: Remove what does not serve the message.
A simpler design or sentence still needs the key information.
Concision communicates the needed meaning with economical wording.

notes: Shorter is not automatically better. Do not remove a necessary date, place, or qualification.
The requested short model is one good edit, not the only grammatical invitation.

levels.A2: Keep what he did and why. Remove in order.
levels.B1: To calm himself states the purpose; in order adds no extra meaning in this sentence.
levels.B2: Concision preserves the action and motivation. It does not remove information simply to make every sentence short.

function.bridge: A design serves a purpose. Narrative, explanation, and argument organize prose for different purposes.
before: When the power failed, the room fell silent. Then Mina lit a candle.
after: A mains-powered lamp goes out when its electricity supply is interrupted.

game.prompt: Your paragraph’s job is to explain a cause and result, rather than tell a particular story. Choose the explanatory sentence.
tiles: When the power failed, the room fell silent. Then Mina lit a candle.
A mains-powered lamp goes out when its electricity supply is interrupted.
We should prepare for power failures so that work can continue.
game.reason: The selected sentence explains how loss of supply affects a lamp. The first recounts a scene; the third argues for action.

vocab.meaning: Both ask who needs the message and what they should do or understand.
A notice, CV, and story have different conventions and jobs.
Judge the result against the audience’s task, not decoration alone.

notes: These examples compare purposes; they are not interchangeable rewrites with identical information.
The game asks for an explanation. A narrative or argument could be appropriate for a different writing purpose.

levels.A2: Mains-powered means using the electrical supply. Goes out means stops giving light.
levels.B1: A narrative recounts events. An explanation shows how or why. An argument supports a position.
levels.B2: Purpose shapes the organization and register of prose. A single text can combine narrative, exposition, and argument.
